title: Navigation by Map and Compass - Military Method
source: U.S. Army TC 3-25.26 / U.S. Marine Corps / NOAA NCEI
summary: The Army and Marine Corps method for land navigation adapted for civilians: reading the map margin, converting between grid and magnetic azimuths, pace counting, resection, intersection, and planning legs with attack points and catching features.

steps.title: Read the margin and orient the map
steps.body: Start with the map margin: scale, contour interval, grid zone, and the declination diagram showing true north, grid north, and magnetic north. The angle between grid north and magnetic north is the G-M angle. To orient with a compass, lay its straight edge along a north-south grid line with the top toward the top of the map, then turn the map and compass together until the needle sits at the G-M angle shown in the diagram. To orient by terrain, line up two linear features - a road and a stream, for example - with the real ones in front of you. Two features keep you from orienting the map backwards.

steps.title: Get current declination - and get the direction right
steps.body: Magnetic declination changes over time, so the number printed on an old map can be several degrees off. Look up your location on NOAA's declination calculator (World Magnetic Model 2025, valid through 2029). East declination means the needle points east of true north; west means it points west. In late 2026 the model gives roughly 15 degrees east near Seattle, about 9 degrees east in eastern Montana, near zero across the central Plains, about 8 degrees west in central North Carolina, and about 14 degrees west near Boston. The western U.S. has east declination; the eastern U.S. has west declination. Many old manuals and charts get this backwards - check before you trust them.

steps.title: Convert between map and compass
steps.body: A bearing measured on the map is a grid (or true) azimuth; your compass reads magnetic. Map to compass: if magnetic north is east (right) of grid north, subtract the G-M angle; if west (left), add it. Compass to map: do the opposite. The Army memory aid is LARS for map-to-compass: Left Add, Right Subtract. Example in central North Carolina, G-M angle about 8 degrees west: a map bearing of 090 becomes a compass bearing of 098. In Seattle, about 15 degrees east: a map bearing of 090 becomes 075. Always re-check the sign with the diagram; if your compass has adjustable declination, set it once and skip the math.

steps.title: Measure and shoot azimuths
steps.body: On the map, draw a line from your position to the target, lay a protractor or the compass baseplate along it with north aligned to a grid line, and read the grid azimuth. Convert to magnetic. On the ground, use the compass-to-cheek method on a lensatic compass for accuracy, or center-hold for speed and darkness. Stay clear of metal: Marine Corps training lists about 55 m from high-tension lines, 18 m from vehicles, 10 m from barbed wire, 2 m from a machine gun, and half a meter from a rifle. Back azimuth: add 180 if under 180, subtract 180 if 180 or more.

steps.title: Count paces and track them
steps.body: A pace is one full stride, counted each time the same foot strikes - about 30 inches for an average soldier. Marine training gives an average of 60 to 75 paces per 100 m; walk a measured 100 m course several times to find yours. Your pace shortens going uphill, into wind, on sand, mud, or snow, in rain or snow, in heavy clothing, and in fog or darkness; it lengthens downhill and with a tailwind. Track distance with pace beads: a strand of 9 beads, one moved per 100 m, and a separate strand of 4 beads, one moved per kilometer. After the ninth 100 m bead, the next 100 m completes a kilometer: reset the 9 and move one kilometer bead.

steps.title: Find your location by resection
steps.body: Resection finds where you are from known landmarks. Orient the map. Identify two or three features you can see on both the ground and map, preferably 60 to 120 degrees apart. Shoot a magnetic azimuth to each, convert to grid, then find the back azimuth. From each landmark on the map, draw a line along its back azimuth. Where the lines cross is your position. Three lines usually form a small 'triangle of error' - you are inside it. Modified resection: if you are on a known linear feature, like a road or river, one back-azimuth line crossing that feature gives your position.

steps.title: Locate a distant point by intersection
steps.body: Intersection finds an unknown point you can see, such as smoke, a signal, or a vehicle, from two known positions. From your first known spot, shoot an azimuth to the object, convert to grid, and draw that line on the map from your position. Move to a second known spot well to one side - ideally so the two lines cross at a wide angle - and repeat. Where the lines cross is the object. This is how you can give rescuers or your group a location for something you cannot reach.

steps.title: Plan legs with attack points and catching features
steps.body: The combination method uses both terrain and compass. Pick an attack point - an easy-to-find feature, ideally within about 400 m of your goal. Note collecting features along the way to check progress. Choose a catching feature past your goal, like a road or stream, so you know you overshot; if none exists, stop when you reach 150 percent of the planned pace count. For a goal on a linear feature, aim a few degrees to one side on purpose (deliberate offset) so you know which way to turn when you hit it.

warnings: Using the wrong sign for declination doubles your error instead of removing it. In the western U.S., magnetic north is east of true north; in the eastern U.S., it is west. Confirm with NOAA's calculator.
Declination printed on old maps can be badly outdated. Use the current World Magnetic Model value.
Misidentifying a landmark during resection produces a confident but wrong position. Use three landmarks and check that the result matches the terrain around you.
proTips: Write your pace count and current declination on tape on the compass.
Practice resection from your own neighborhood using water towers, radio towers, and church steeples.
When you report a location, state the grid zone or datum and how you got it, for example 'six-digit grid from resection, about 100 m accuracy.'

whenNotTo: Do not attempt long cross-country legs in bad weather or darkness if you can wait for better conditions.
Do not leave a safe position to navigate if you are injured, exhausted, or unsure of your start point - stay put and signal (see nav-008).

quickGlance.situation: You must navigate with a topographic map and compass to a specific point, with no GPS.
immediate: Orient the map with a compass or two linear features
Get current declination; west U.S. is east declination, east U.S. is west declination
Map to compass: Left (west) Add, Right (east) Subtract
then: Track distance with pace count and pace beads
Use resection to fix your position and an attack point plus catching feature to find the goal
